q-75921.name: Question 1
q-75921.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=0$ is an excluded solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

We multiply both sides of the equation by $2x,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{2x}+\frac{x-4}{2x} & =\frac{5x-6}{2x} \\ 2x\cdot (\frac{x-2}{2x}+\frac{x-4}{2x}) & =n\cdot (\frac{5x-6}{2x}) \\ 2x\cdot \frac{x-2}{2x}+2x\cdot \frac{x-4}{2x} & =2x\cdot \frac{5x-6}{2x} \\ \cancel{2x}\cdot \frac{x-2}{\cancel{2x}}+\cancel{2x}\cdot \frac{x-4}{\cancel{2x}} & =\cancel{2x}\cdot \frac{5x-6}{\cancel{2x}} \\ x-2+x-4 & =5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2+x-4 & =5x-6 \\ 2x-6 & =5x-6 \\ 5x-2x & =-6+6 \\ 3x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. Therefore, we conclude that there is no solution.

q-270354.name: Question 2
q-270354.worked_solution:
First, we note that $b=0$ is an excluded solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

We multiply both sides of the equation by $b,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{b+5}{b}+\frac{b-7}{b} & =6 \\ b\cdot (\frac{b+5}{b}+\frac{b-7}{b}) & =b\cdot 6 \\ b\cdot \frac{b+5}{b}+b\cdot \frac{b-7}{b} & =b\cdot 6 \\ \cancel{b}\cdot \frac{b+5}{\cancel{b}}+\cancel{b}\cdot \frac{b-7}{\cancel{b}} & =b\cdot 6 \\ b+5+b-7 & =6b\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $b,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}b+5+b-7 & =6b \\ 2b-2 & =6b \\ -4b & =2 \\ b & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $b=0$ as a solution. However, since $b=-\frac{1}{2}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $b=-\frac{1}{2}.$

q-3518.name: Question 3
q-3518.worked_solution:
We note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined.

The equation has the denominators $x$ and $3x.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(x,3x)=3x.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $3x,$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x\cdot (\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{x}) & =3x\cdot (\frac{3-x}{3x}) \\ 3x\cdot \frac{2}{3}+3x\cdot \frac{1}{x} & =3x\cdot \frac{3-x}{3x} \\ \cancel{3}x\cdot \frac{2}{\cancel{3}}+3\cancel{x}\cdot \frac{1}{\cancel{x}} & =\cancel{3x}\cdot \frac{3-x}{\cancel{3x}} \\ x\cdot (2)+3\cdot (1) & =3-x \\ 2x+3 & =3-x\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+3 & =3-x \\ 2x+x & =3-3 \\ 3x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. Since $x=0,$ we conclude that there is no solution.

q-115795.name: Question 4
q-115795.worked_solution:
We note that $q=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $3q$ and $4q.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(3q,4q)=12q.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $12q,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2q-1}{4q} & =\frac{q+1}{3q}-1 \\ 12q\cdot (\frac{2q-1}{4q}) & =12q\cdot (\frac{q+1}{3q}-1) \\ 12q\cdot \frac{2q-1}{4q} & =12q\cdot \frac{q+1}{3q}-12q\cdot 1 \\ 3\cdot \cancel{4q}\cdot (\frac{2q-1}{\cancel{4q}}) & =4\cdot \cancel{3q}\cdot (\frac{q+1}{\cancel{3q}})-12q \\ 3(2q-1) & =4(q+1)-12q\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $q,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3(2q-1) & =4(q+1)-12q \\ 6q-3 & =4q+4-12q \\ 6q-3 & =-8q+4 \\ 6q+8q & =4+3 \\ 14q & =7 \\ q & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $q=0$ as a solution. But since $q=\frac{1}{2}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $q=\frac{1}{2}.$

q-276864.name: Question 5
q-276864.worked_solution:
We note that $f=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $f,\,2f,$ and $5f.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(f,2f,5f)=10f.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $10f,$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f+6}{f}-\frac{3f+9}{5f} & =\frac{f+2}{2f} \\ 10f(\frac{f+6}{f}-\frac{3f+9}{5f}) & =10f(\frac{f+2}{2f}) \\ 10f\cdot \frac{f+6}{f}-10f\cdot \frac{3f+9}{5f} & =10f\cdot \frac{f+2}{2f} \\ 10\cdot f\cdot \frac{f+6}{f}-2\cdot 5f\cdot \frac{3f+9}{5f} & =5\cdot 2f\cdot \frac{f+2}{2f} \\ 10\cdot \cancel{f}\cdot \frac{f+6}{\cancel{f}}-2\cdot \cancel{5f}\cdot \frac{3f+9}{\cancel{5f}} & =5\cdot \cancel{2f}\cdot \frac{f+2}{\cancel{2f}} \\ 10(f+6)-2(3f+9) & =5(f+2)\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $f,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}10(f+6)-2(3f+9) & =5(f+2) \\ 10f+60-6f-18 & =5f+10 \\ 4f+42 & =5f+10 \\ -f & =-32 \\ f & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $f=0$ as a solution. But since $f=32\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $f=32.$

q-75936.name: Question 6
q-75936.problem: Which value of $m$ satisfies the equation $\frac{4m+1}{3m}-\frac{m-1}{6m}=\frac{1}{9m}?$
q-75936.worked_solution:
We note that $m=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $3m,6m,$ and $9m.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(3m,6m,9m)=18m.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $18m,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4m+1}{3m}-\frac{m-1}{6m} & =\frac{1}{9m} \\ 18m\cdot (\frac{4m+1}{3m}-\frac{m-1}{6m}) & =18m\cdot (\frac{1}{9m}) \\ 18m\cdot (\frac{4m+1}{3m})-18m\cdot (\frac{m-1}{6m}) & =18m\cdot (\frac{1}{9m}) \\ 6\cdot 3m\cdot (\frac{4m+1}{3m})-3\cdot 6m\cdot (\frac{m-1}{6m}) & =2\cdot 9m\cdot (\frac{1}{9m}) \\ 6\cdot \cancel{3m}\cdot (\frac{4m+1}{\cancel{3m}})-3\cdot \cancel{6m}\cdot (\frac{m-1}{\cancel{6m}}) & =2\cdot \cancel{9m}\cdot (\frac{1}{\cancel{9m}}) \\ 6(4m+1)-3(m-1) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $m,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6(4m+1)-3(m-1) & =2 \\ 24m+6-3m+3 & =2 \\ 21m+9 & =2 \\ 21m & =-7 \\ m & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $m=0$ as a solution. But since $m=-\frac{1}{3}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $m=-\frac{1}{3}.$

a
12
b
−16
c

−13

Correct
EXPLANATION

We note that m=0 cannot be a solution since division by 0 is undefined.

The equation has the denominators 3m,6m, and 9m. So first, we find the least common multiple (or LCM) of the denominators. We find that

LCM(3m,6m,9m)=18m.

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by 18m, and simplify:

4m+13m−m−16m=19m18m⋅(4m+13m−m−16m)=18m⋅(19m)18m⋅(4m+13m)−18m⋅(m−16m)=18m⋅(19m)6⋅3m⋅(4m+13m)−3⋅6m⋅(m−16m)=2⋅9m⋅(19m)6⋅3m⋅(4m+13m)−3⋅6m⋅(m−16m)=2⋅9m⋅(19m)6(4m+1)−3(m−1)=2

We now have a linear equation in m, and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

6(4m+1)−3(m−1)=224m+6−3m+3=221m+9=221m=−7m=−13

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow m=0 as a solution. But since m=−13≠0, we conclude that the solution is m=−13.

q-75955.name: Question 7
q-75955.problem: Which value of $n$ satisfies the equation $\frac{3}{2n}-\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}=\frac{7}{3n}?$
q-75955.worked_solution:
We note that $n=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $2n,$ ${n}^{2},$ and $3n.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(2n,{n}^{2},3n)=6{n}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $6{n}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2n}-\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}} & =\frac{7}{3n} \\ 6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2n}-\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}) & =6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{7}{3n}) \\ 6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2n})-6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}) & =6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{7}{3n}) \\ 3n\cdot 2n\cdot (\frac{3}{2n})-6\cdot {n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}) & =2n\cdot 3n\cdot (\frac{7}{3n}) \\ 3n\cdot \cancel{2n}\cdot (\frac{3}{\cancel{2n}})-6\cdot \cancel{{n}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1-n}{\cancel{{n}^{2}}}) & =2n\cdot \cancel{3n}\cdot (\frac{7}{\cancel{3n}}) \\ 3n\cdot (3)-6\cdot (1-n) & =2n\cdot (7) \\ 9n-6(1-n) & =14n\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $n,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}9n-6(1-n) & =14n \\ 15n-6 & =14n \\ n & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $n=0$ as a solution. But since $n=6\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $n=6.$

32n−1−nn2=73n6n2⋅(32n−1−nn2)=6n2⋅(73n)6n2⋅(32n)−6n2⋅(1−nn2)=6n2⋅(73n)3n⋅2n⋅(32n)−6⋅n2⋅(1−nn2)=2n⋅3n⋅(73n)3n⋅2n⋅(32n)−6⋅n2⋅(1−nn2)=2n⋅3n⋅(73n)3n⋅(3)−6⋅(1−n)=2n⋅(7)9n−6(1−n)=14n

q-276869.name: Question 8
q-276869.worked_solution:
We note that $v=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $6v,\,{v}^{2},$ and $2{v}^{2}.$ First, we find the denominators' least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$). We have that

$$
\text{LCM}(6v,{v}^{2},2{v}^{2})=6{v}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $6{v}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{v+4}{{v}^{2}}-\frac{7}{6v} & =\frac{5}{2{v}^{2}} \\ 6{v}^{2}(\frac{v+4}{{v}^{2}}-\frac{7}{6v}) & =6{v}^{2}(\frac{5}{2{v}^{2}}) \\ 6{v}^{2}\cdot \frac{v+4}{{v}^{2}}-6{v}^{2}\cdot \frac{7}{6v} & =6{v}^{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2{v}^{2}} \\ 6\cdot {v}^{2}\cdot \frac{v+4}{{v}^{2}}-6v\cdot v\cdot \frac{7}{6v} & =3\cdot 2{v}^{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2{v}^{2}} \\ 6\cdot \cancel{{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{v+4}{\cancel{{v}^{2}}}-\cancel{6v}\cdot v\cdot \frac{7}{\cancel{6v}} & =3\cdot \cancel{2{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{5}{\cancel{2{v}^{2}}} \\ 6(v+4)-v\cdot (7) & =3\cdot 5 \\ 6(v+4)-7v & =15\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $v,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6(v+4)-7v & =15 \\ 6v+24-7v & =15 \\ -v+24 & =15 \\ -v & =-9 \\ v & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $v=0$ as a solution. But since $v=9\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $v=9.$
